title: Tunable responsivity and bandwidth in microwave kinetic inductance detectors via readout current nonlinearity
authors: Maclean Rouble, Peter Day, Matt Dobbs, Joshua Montgomery, Sofiia Savchyn, Graeme Smecher
abstract: Microwave kinetic inductance detectors (MKIDs) are generally read out with microwave readout tones of high enough amplitude to adequately suppress the noise contribution of the first-stage amplifier. At high readout power, the detector's resonant frequency is altered as a result of the dependence of the kinetic inductance on the internally circulating microwave current. With the tone placed below the resonant frequency, the nonlinear frequency shift results in a positive feedback effect that can significantly enhance the responsivity of the detector, to both optical and microwave power. We report a factor of 10 enhancement in optical response by tuning the readout power and frequency to close to the resonator's bifurcation point. A corresponding decrease in the bandwidth of the resonator is observed under these conditions. We show that the strength of the feedback effect can be easily selected by adjusting the excitation, and provide a map of possible operational states to do so. Operation of MKIDs in this mode could be used to improve sensitivity when non-intrinsic noise sources are significant.
summary: This paper investigates using the inherent nonlinearity in Microwave Kinetic Inductance Detectors (MKIDs) as a controllable resource. By tuning the readout power near resonance bifurcation points, the authors achieve significant enhancements in detector responsivity. This work is crucial for improving cryogenic sensor sensitivity by mastering nonlinear operational regimes.
main_problem: The research aims to utilize the inherent nonlinearity of Microwave Kinetic Inductance Detectors (MKIDs) by controlling the readout current to achieve tunable responsivity and bandwidth enhancement.
main_result: By operating near the resonator's bifurcation point, a factor of 10 enhancement in optical response was demonstrated, although this comes at the cost of reduced bandwidth.
method: The authors developed a theoretical framework based on analyzing the nonlinear steady-state response of the driven resonator, complemented by experimental measurements of noise spectra under varying bias conditions.
model_or_system: The system is an MKID array composed of superconducting resonators whose kinetic inductance depends nonlinearly on the circulating microwave current. The physics is modeled using a coupled optical cavity approach describing the steady-state photon number balance.
key_observables: Responsivity (both optical and microwave), bandwidth, resonant frequency shift ($\delta x$), and noise spectrum characteristics (white noise level, roll-off frequency).
important_parameters: Readout power ($P_g$), detuning ($x_0$), quality factors ($Q_r, Q_c$), and the nonlinear current scale ($I^*$).
main_assumptions: The analysis simplifies by focusing on reactive inductance changes ($\delta L_k \propto I^2$) while ignoring pair-breaking energy effects. The system is modeled as a one-port optical cavity coupled to a three-port network.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup, power sweep responses showing bistability/hysteresis near bifurcation points, and noise spectra confirming enhanced white noise levels and reduced roll-off frequency with increased nonlinear bias.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing MKIDs' nonlinearity as a resource, developing the theoretical model for controlled operation via $(x_0, P_g)$, demonstrating responsivity enhancement through bifurcation analysis, and finally validating these effects by analyzing noise spectra changes.
why_interesting: This work provides an excellent example of how nonlinear classical physics (bifurcation theory) can be applied to enhance the sensitivity of quantum-limited detectors, drawing parallels between driven resonator dynamics and open quantum system response functions.
